clinicalPearls: Primary dysmenorrhoea is painful menstruation without underlying pelvic pathology and typically begins within a year or two of menarche once ovulatory cycles are established
Secondary dysmenorrhoea arises from identifiable pelvic disease, most often endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, or pelvic inflammatory disease, and tends to begin later or change in character
The pain of primary dysmenorrhoea is cramping and suprapubic, often radiating to the back and thighs, and coincides with the onset of menstrual flow
Prostaglandin-driven myometrial contractions and uterine ischaemia underlie primary dysmenorrhoea, which explains the effectiveness of prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors
First-line management combines non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with hormonal suppression of ovulation such as combined hormonal contraception
Features suggesting secondary causes include pain that starts before bleeding or persists after it, deep dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, or poor response to standard treatment
A careful history and examination, with pelvic ultrasound and consideration of laparoscopy, help identify secondary pathology when suspected
Symptoms of primary dysmenorrhoea often improve with age and after childbirth
reference.pathophysiology: In primary dysmenorrhoea, the fall in progesterone at the end of the luteal phase triggers release of arachidonic acid and increased endometrial production of prostaglandins, particularly PGF2-alpha. These stimulate intense, poorly coordinated myometrial contractions that raise intrauterine pressure and reduce uterine blood flow, producing ischaemic pain analogous to angina; leukotrienes and vasopressin contribute. In secondary dysmenorrhoea the pain results instead from a structural or inflammatory disorder such as ectopic endometrial tissue, myometrial invasion by endometrium, leiomyomas, or infection.
additionalInvestigations: Focused history and pelvic examination to distinguish primary from secondary causes
Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound to assess for fibroids, adenomyosis, and adnexal pathology
Screening for sexually transmitted infection where pelvic inflammatory disease is suspected
Diagnostic laparoscopy when endometriosis is suspected and symptoms persist
Pregnancy test to exclude pregnancy-related pain
redFlags: Pain beginning well after menarche or changing markedly in character, suggesting secondary pathology
Associated abnormal or heavy uterine bleeding
Deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, or cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms suggesting endometriosis
Fever, abnormal discharge, or pelvic tenderness suggesting infection
Failure to respond to first-line therapy, warranting further evaluation
reference.prognosis: Primary dysmenorrhoea is benign and commonly improves over time and after childbirth, with most women achieving good symptom control from anti-inflammatory and hormonal treatment. The prognosis of secondary dysmenorrhoea depends on the underlying condition, and outcomes improve when that cause is correctly identified and managed.
pitfalls: Assuming all menstrual pain is primary and missing endometriosis or adenomyosis
Failing to reassess when standard treatment does not work
Overlooking pelvic inflammatory disease as a treatable secondary cause
Not offering hormonal suppression alongside anti-inflammatory therapy
Attributing new-onset severe pain in an older woman to simple period pain
management: Give non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs as prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors, started with the onset of menses, to counter prostaglandin-driven myometrial contraction and ischaemia
Suppress ovulation with combined hormonal contraception, a progestogen, or the levonorgestrel intrauterine system for those wanting contraception or needing more control
Advise adjunctive non-pharmacological measures such as local heat and exercise, with reassurance in primary dysmenorrhoea
Investigate and treat the underlying cause in secondary dysmenorrhoea, including endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids and pelvic inflammatory disease
Treat suspected pelvic inflammatory disease with appropriate antibiotics and refer for diagnostic laparoscopy where endometriosis is suspected
Exclude pregnancy-related pain before attributing symptoms to dysmenorrhoea
Refer to gynaecology when pain is refractory, atypical, or has features suggesting secondary pathology
